1H (Number Theory)

Words: 236 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 236
1H OurBigBook.com
A reduced positive definite binary quadratic form ax2+bxy+cy2 satisfies ∣b∣≤a≤c, with b≥0 when ∣b∣=a or a=c. These inequalities select representatives under proper equivalence of binary quadratic forms; the changes of variables have integer entries and determinant 1.
For the first binary quadratic form, put x=u−v, y=v. For the second, put x=−u−3v, y=u+2v. Both changes preserve coprime integers, and give
f=3u2+2uv+4v2=3(u+v/3)2+311​v2,g=u2+11v2.
(1)
Proper representation means using gcd(u,v)=1. For f, ∣v∣≥2 gives a value greater than 5, while v=0 forces u=±1. For ∣v∣=1, the smallest values are 4 and 5. For g, v=0 again gives only 1 primitively; ∣v∣=1 gives 11,12,15,…, and ∣v∣≥2 gives at least 44. Thus the three smallest properly represented values are
f:3,4,5;g:1,11,12.​
(2)
For example the original variables can be chosen as (1,0),(−1,1),(−2,1) for f, and (−1,1),(−3,2),(−4,3) for g.
Every positive definite binary quadratic form can be reduced: integer shears first make ∣b∣≤a, and interchanging the variables when c<a decreases the positive leading coefficient, so this procedure terminates. To enumerate the reduced forms of discriminant minus forty-four, reduction gives 3a2≤44, hence 1≤a≤3. Checking b2−4ac=−44 with the reduced inequalities gives exactly
(1,0,11),(2,2,6),(3,2,4),(3,−2,4).
(3)
The second represents only even integers. The last two have the same represented values, by u↦−u. The first and third are the reduced versions of g and f. Therefore every represented odd integer occurs in at least one of f,g, whether or not its original representation was primitive.

Let A be the closure of the polynomials in C(K) for the uniform norm. It is a closed algebra, since products of uniformly convergent sequences converge uniformly on the compact set K.
Choose a point W with ∣W∣>supz∈K​∣z∣. The uniformly convergent geometric series
W−z1​=∑j=0∞​Wj+1zj​
(4)
shows that this reciprocal belongs to A. Join w to W by a continuous path in C∖K. Its image is compact and disjoint from K, so their distance d is positive. Partition the path into finitely many steps shorter than d/2.
Suppose 1/(b−z)∈A and ∣a−b∣<d/2, with b on the path. Then
a−z1​=∑j=0∞​(b−z)j+1(b−a)j​
(5)
converges uniformly on K, since ∣b−z∣≥d. Every partial sum belongs to A, by its algebra property, and so does the limit. Working backwards along the partition transfers the pole from W to w. Thus 1/(w−z)∈A: a polynomial P exists with
z∈Ksup​​P(z)−w−z1​​<ϵ.​
(6)
This pole-moving polynomial approximation is the elementary mechanism behind the polynomial Runge theorem.

Order the prescribed lengths as l1​≤⋯≤lN​. Construct a prefix code on the binary tree. At depth li​, previously assigned codewords exclude ∑j<i​2li​−lj​ of the 2li​ vertices. The Kraft inequality implies
∑j<i​2li​−lj​+1≤2li​,
(7)
so an available vertex can be assigned to the next symbol. None of the assigned words is a prefix of another. Reading each word up to the next assigned vertex gives unique decoding, so this constructs the required uniquely decodable code.
For completeness the same length inequality is necessary even for a uniquely decodable code which is not a prefix code. Write K=∑a​2−l(a) and L=maxa​l(a). For r successive symbols, distinct symbol strings have distinct concatenated codewords. At total length j there are at most 2j such strings. Therefore
Kr=∑j=rrL​Nj​2−j≤rL.
(8)
Taking rth roots and letting r→∞ gives K≤1. This is the McMillan inequality.
Set q(a)=2−l(a)/K. The relative entropy inequality gives
El(A)−H(A)=∑a​p(a)log2​q(a)p(a)​−log2​K≥0.
(9)
Here Shannon entropy uses base 2, with 0log0=0. The relative entropy is nonnegative, with equality precisely when the two probability distributions coincide; this follows from logt≤t−1. Consequently equality holds exactly when
K=1andp(a)=2−l(a) for every a.​
(10)
In particular all alphabet symbols must have positive probability for equality with finite prescribed lengths.

4J OurBigBook.com
The command fits the simple linear regression
Yi​=β0​+β1​ti​+εi​,εi​ independent N(0,σ2),
(11)
using ordinary least squares. The fitted conditional mean is a straight line in time. The regression residuals are mainly positive at the beginning and end and negative in the middle, so the mean function needs curvature.
A direct improvement is polynomial regression of degree two:
fit2 <- lm(Counts ~ Time + I(Time^2), data = geiger)
anova(fit1, fit2)
The nested-model F-test tests H0​:β2​=0 against a nonzero quadratic coefficient. If N measurements were used, its statistic is
F=RSS2​/(N−3)RSS1​−RSS2​​∼F1,N−3​under H0​.​
(12)
A small reported p-value supports the quadratic term. The new regression residuals should then be checked for remaining systematic structure, changing variance and temporal dependence, because the F-test assumes independent errors of common variance. Radioactive decay also motivates an exponential mean, but the displayed curvature already justifies this simple nested comparison.

There are kxn​ seeds and their germinating proportion is e−γxn​, giving the survival-augmented Ricker map with zero survival. A positive equilibrium point satisfies e−γx∗​=1/k, so
x∗​=γlogk​,F′(x∗​)=1−logk.
(13)
It exists when k>1 and is strictly linearly stable when ∣1−logk∣<1. Thus the usual strict linear-stability interval is 1<k<e2​.
With winter survival, surviving adults and new plants add:
xn+1​=sxn​+kxn​e−γxn​,x∗​=γ1​log1−sk​.
(14)
Writing L=log[k/(1−s)], the linearization of a dynamical system has multiplier 1−(1−s)L. Hence the strict linear-stability interval becomes
1−s<k<(1−s)exp(1−s2​).​
(15)
Its lower endpoint is less than 1. Its upper endpoint exceeds e2: for t=1−s∈(0,1), logt+2/t is decreasing in t and equals 2 at t=1.
The nonlinear stability at the Ricker flip threshold needs a separate check. The upper endpoints have multiplier −1, so the strict linear test alone does not decide stability there. They are in fact locally asymptotically stable, with algebraic rather than geometric convergence. To see this, put u=γ(x−x∗​) at L=2/(1−s). The local map is
u⟼−u+su2+(21−s​−31​)u3+O(u4),
(16)
and its second iterate is u−2(s2−s/2+1/6)u3+O(u4). The cubic coefficient in parentheses is positive for every s∈[0,1). Thus, if “stable” includes nonlinear endpoint stability, the upper inequalities can be replaced by ≤; the lower endpoints have no positive equilibrium.

limR→∞​limϵ↓0​(∫−R−a−ϵ​+∫−a+ϵa−ϵ​+∫a+ϵR​)x2−a2cosx​dx.

Resa​z2−a2eiz​=2aeia​,Res−a​z2−a2eiz​=−2ae−ia​,

The Hamiltonian is H(q,p)=p2/(2m)+V(q)​. On a regular family of closed phase-space trajectories, action-angle variables are canonical coordinates (θ,I) in which θ is periodic modulo 2π and H=H(I). Hamilton's equations then give I˙=0 and θ˙=dH/dI.
The action variable is
I=2π1​∮pdq=π1​∫q−​q+​​2m(E−V(q))​dq.​
(20)
The orientation is that of the motion, so the integral is the positive enclosed phase-space area divided by 2π.

A constant-energy phase-space trajectory of the harmonic oscillator is the ellipse
2E/(mω2)q2​+2mEp2​=1.
(21)
Its area is π2E/(mω2)​2mE​=2πE/ω. Thus the action and slow energy change are
I=E/ω,E(t)≃Iω(t).​
(22)
The action variable is an adiabatic invariant when ∣ω˙∣≪ω2, with ω staying positive. Averaging over many short oscillations therefore keeps I approximately fixed; an increase in frequency increases the energy in the same proportion.

The flatness problem is the extreme closeness to spatial flatness required in the early universe if ordinary decelerating expansion is to produce the observed near-flat universe. From the Friedmann equation, with c=1 and curvature constant k,
H2=38πG​ρ−a2k​,Ω−1=a2H2k​=a˙2k​.
(23)
During decelerating expansion ∣Ω−1∣ grows. The Friedmann acceleration equation gives a¨/a=−4πG(ρ+3P)/3. Thus ρ+3P<0 makes an expanding universe accelerate, increases a˙ and suppresses ∣Ω−1∣: this is the inflationary solution of the flatness problem.
The slow-roll approximation neglects ϕ˙​2/2 compared with V and ϕ¨​ compared with 3Hϕ˙​. For the positive-field branch, taking m>0,
H≃3​mϕ​,3Hϕ˙​≃−2m2ϕ,ϕ˙​≃−3​2m​.
(24)
Integrating the field equation and a˙/a=H gives the slow-roll solution
ϕ(t)=ϕi​−3​2mt​,a(t)=ai​exp(3​mϕi​t​−3m2t2​)=ai​exp4ϕi2​−ϕ(t)2​.​
(25)
The potential slow-roll parameters are ϵV​=ηV​=2/ϕ2. They cease to be small when ϕ is of order 1 in these units; the customary endpoint ϵV​=1 is ϕend​≃2​​. Equating the approximate kinetic and potential energies instead gives 2/3​, another order-one indicator, not a precise endpoint of an approximation that is already failing.

10I OurBigBook.com
Work in the complete Banach space C([0,1]) with the uniform norm. Each Em​ is closed. Indeed if fj​→f uniformly and xj​ witnesses membership in Em​, pass to a subsequence with xj​→x. For each y∈[0,1], uniform convergence and continuity give
∣f(y)−f(x)∣=limj​∣fj​(y)−fj​(xj​)∣≤m∣y−x∣α.
(31)
Thus x witnesses membership for f.
Each Em​ has empty interior. Approximate an arbitrary f uniformly by a piecewise linear function q on a uniform mesh, and let D bound the absolute slopes of q. On a sufficiently fine uniform refinement of mesh δ, add a triangular oscillation of fixed small amplitude b, alternating between b and −b at successive vertices. The resulting function g is still as close to f as desired, and every segment has absolute slope at least 2b/δ−D. For any x, choose the farther endpoint of a segment containing x. Its distance h is between δ/2 and δ, so
∣h∣α∣g(x+h)−g(x)∣​≥(2b/δ−D)δ1−αmin(1,2α−1)>m
(32)
when δ is small. Therefore g∈/Em​.
By the Baire category theorem, the complement of ⋃m​Em​ is dense and nonempty. If the local limsup in the question were finite at some x, its nearby differences would satisfy a finite bound. The remaining differences, with ∣h∣≥δ>0, are bounded by 2∥f∥∞​δ−α. Combining the bounds would put f in some Em​, a contradiction. Hence the required limsup is infinite at every point, including one-sided approaches at the endpoints.

a OurBigBook.com
Let N=x+y. Uninfected births and density limitation give x(1−N), while horizontal transmission transfers individuals to the infected class at rate βxy. Infected births are infected by vertical transmission, and their net demographic growth is y(1−N)−dy. Consequently
x˙=x(1−N)−βxy=x[1−x−(1+β)y],y˙​=y(1−N)−dy+βxy.
(35)
These give the stated equations. Adding them gives N˙=N(1−N)−dy, displaying the additional mortality due to disease.

b OurBigBook.com
At the disease-free equilibrium point (1,0), the linearization of a dynamical system of the infected equation is y˙​=(β−d)y. Thus exponential invasion occurs exactly when β>d​. At equality there is no positive linear growth rate; the nonlinear boundary dynamics described below do not give sustained invasion.

c OurBigBook.com
Assume first β>0 and d≥0. The nonnegative equilibrium points are
O=(0,0),U=(1,0),I=(0,1−d)(d≤1),
(36)
and, when both coordinates are nonnegative,
C=(β2d(1+β)−β​,β2β−d​).
(37)
The Jacobian matrix at O has eigenvalues 1,1−d, so O cannot attract an initially positive uninfected population. At U the eigenvalues are −1,β−d. At I, for d<1, they are d(1+β)−β and −(1−d). At an interior C, the equilibrium equations reduce the Jacobian matrix to
(−x∗​−(1−β)y∗​​−(1+β)x∗​−y∗​​),trJ=−x∗​−y∗​<0,detJ=β2x∗​y∗​>0.
(38)
Thus the coexistence equilibrium is asymptotically stable precisely when β/(1+β)<d<β.
For positive initial populations these local results identify the global outcome. The relation N˙=N(1−N)−dy bounds all trajectories. With the Dulac function 1/(xy), the divergence of the rescaled vector field is −1/y−1/x<0, excluding interior periodic orbits. Boundary saddles cannot attract an interior trajectory except at the merging thresholds. The resulting long-term outcomes are
0≤d<β/(1+β)β/(1+β)<d<βd>β​: I (all infected),: C (coexistence),: U (disease disappears).​​
(39)
At d=β/(1+β), C merges into I; at d=β, it merges into U. The merged equilibria still attract interior trajectories, but convergence along the zero-eigenvalue direction is algebraic. For example at d=β, put x=1+u, y=v. The local centre manifold has u=−(1+β)v+O(v2), and v˙=−β2v2+O(v3). At the other threshold, using y=(1−d)+v, x=u, gives v=(β−1)u+O(u2) and u˙=−β2u2+O(u3).
The invariant axes also matter: y=0 leads to U whenever x(0)>0; x=0 leads to I for d<1 and to extinction for d≥1. At d=1, I coincides with O. If β=0, disease declines for d>0 and any initially positive x tends to U. If also d=0, every point x+y=1 is an equilibrium and the initial population proportions are preserved.

d OurBigBook.com
For β>0 and positive initial populations, summing the coordinates of the attracting equilibrium point gives the steady total population
N∗​(d)=⎩⎨⎧​1−d,d/β,1,​0≤d≤β/(1+β),β/(1+β)≤d≤β,d≥β.​​
(40)
Its minimum is 1/(1+β) at d=β/(1+β). Small mortality leaves a fully infected population with only modest demographic loss. Raising mortality first reduces that population; after the threshold it suppresses infection sufficiently for the uninfected population to recover. Beyond the invasion threshold the disease cannot persist.

12C OurBigBook.com
The terms in the Boltzmann equation respectively describe dilution by expansion, pair annihilation, and pair production from the thermal bath. The annihilation rate per volume is ⟨σv⟩nnˉ; P(t) is the corresponding production rate. Antiparticles satisfy the same equation with n replaced by nˉ. Subtracting gives
dtd(n−nˉ)​=−3H(n−nˉ),(n−nˉ)a3=constant.​
(41)
Initial particle-antiparticle symmetry therefore persists. Detailed balance in the thermal bath gives P=⟨σv⟩neq2​, so
dtd(na3)​=⟨σv⟩(neq2​−n2)a3.
(42)
During radiation domination, with fixed effective relativistic degrees of freedom, T∝a−1 and H=Hm​/x2. Thus x˙=Hx and the dilution terms cancel in Y=n/T3:
Y˙=−⟨σv⟩T3(Y2−Yeq2​),dxdY​=−Hm​x2m3⟨σv⟩​(Y2−Yeq2​).​
(43)
After cosmological particle freeze-out, neglect Yeq​. For constant λ the exact reduced solution is
Y(x)1​=Yf​1​+λ(xf​1​−x1​),Y∞​=(Yf​1​+xf​λ​)−1.​
(44)
For the post-freeze-out relic abundance, the familiar answer Y∞​≃xf​/λ additionally neglects 1/Yf​ compared with λ/xf​. It is an approximation, not an exact consequence of the post-freeze-out equation without initial data. A smaller annihilation cross-section means smaller λ, earlier decoupling and less depletion, so weakly interacting particles normally have a larger relic abundance.

i OurBigBook.com
Zorn lemma states that a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain in a partial order has an upper bound has a maximal element. Here is a proof from the axiom of choice and Hartogs theorem.
Suppose there is no maximal element. Every chain C has a strict upper bound: choose an upper bound b and then an element strictly greater than b. The family of sets of strict upper bounds is a set of nonempty subsets of the underlying set P. The axiom of choice is used here to choose, simultaneously for every chain C, one strict upper bound b(C).
By Hartogs theorem there is an ordinal κ admitting no injection into P. Transfinite recursion defines xα​ for α<κ by
xα​=b({xβ​:β<α}).
(45)
At each stage the previous elements form a chain, and xα​ is strictly above every one of them. Hence α↦xα​ is an injection κ→P, a contradiction. Therefore a maximal element exists.

Replace the strict partial order by its reflexive closure ≤. Partially order all partial orders on X extending ≤ by inclusion. A chain has an upper bound given by its union: transitivity and antisymmetry each concern finitely many pairs, which all lie in one member of the chain. By Zorn lemma there is a maximal extension R.
If a,b are incomparable under R, define
R′=R ∪ {(x,y):xRa and bRy}.
(46)
This adds aR′b. It is transitive: composing an old pair with a new one stays in the added set; composing two new pairs would require bRa, which is impossible. It is antisymmetric: an added pair and a reverse old pair would again imply bRa, and two reverse added pairs would do the same. Thus R′ is a larger partial order, contradicting maximality. Therefore R is total, and removing its diagonal gives a total order extending the original strict order.
A well-founded relation has a minimal element in every nonempty subset; with the axiom of choice this is equivalent to having no infinite strictly descending sequence. If an extension is a well-order, its least element in any nonempty subset is minimal for the original relation, so the original order must be well-founded.
However not every total extension need be a well-order. Take the empty strict order on N, which is well-founded. Its extension defined by x≺y if x>y in the usual order is total and has no least element.

A Hamilton cycle is a cycle graph which visits every vertex of a finite graph exactly once, apart from returning to its starting vertex. A graph is Hamiltonian when it contains such a cycle.

degv1​+degvk​≥n>k−1,
(47)
so some index has both marks. The edges at that index close the path into the cycle graph
v1​v2​⋯vi​vk​vk−1​⋯vi+1​v1​.
(48)
The minimum-degree hypothesis also forces the graph to be a connected graph: each component would otherwise have at least n/2+1 vertices. If k<n, an edge from this cycle to an outside vertex would give a longer path by opening the cycle at its incident vertex. Hence k=n, proving the Dirac theorem and Hamiltonicity.
The bound is sharp. For n=2m, take two disjoint copies of Km​, with minimum degree m−1. For n=2m+1, take two copies of Km+1​ sharing exactly one vertex. The minimum degree is m, but the shared vertex is a cut vertex, which no Hamiltonian graph can have. Both constructions have
δ=⌈n/2⌉−1.​

If f is an irreducible polynomial, any two roots α,β have the same minimal polynomial. Thus the map Q(α)→Q(β) carrying α to β is a field embedding. The extension theorem for field embeddings extends it to an embedding of the splitting field L into an algebraic closure. Since L/Q is normal, its image is L, so it is an element of the Galois group.
Conversely, factor f into irreducible factors over Q. An automorphism preserves the vanishing of each factor, so it cannot send a root of one factor to a root of another. Since there are no repeated roots, different factors have disjoint root sets. Transitivity on all roots therefore forces a single irreducible factor. This proves the equivalence.

f(stK​(v))⊆stL​(g(v))

for every vertex v. Equivalently, whenever f(x) lies in the interior of a simplex of L, ∣g∣(x) lies in that simplex. In particular f and ∣g∣ are joined by the simplexwise straight-line homotopy.

The Baire category theorem in the needed version states that a nonempty complete metric space cannot be a countable union of closed sets with empty interior. To prove it, suppose F1​,F2​,… are such sets and start with a nonempty open set U. Inductively choose closed balls Bj​ of positive radius at most 2−j, with B1​⊂U∖F1​ and Bj+1​⊂Bj​∖Fj+1​. This is possible because each complement is open and dense. The centres form a Cauchy sequence; completeness supplies a limit in every closed ball. It lies in U and outside every Fj​, proving the theorem.
Here the sequence spaces are over the real scalars, as required by the Euclidean-plane assertion. Suppose an isometry φ:R2→c0​ existed. On the compact complete space S1×S1, the sets
Fn​={(x,y):∣φn​(x)−φn​(y)∣=∥x−y∥2​}
(58)
are closed. They cover that space: for a nonzero sequence in c0​, the supremum norm is attained at a coordinate; for x=y every coordinate works. By the Baire category theorem, one Fn​ contains a product of open arcs. Shrink the arcs to be disjoint. The real coordinate difference is then continuous and nonzero, so its sign is constant on the product. Thus the chord distance has the separated form
∥x−y∥2​=±(φn​(x)−φn​(y)).
(59)
In particular its alternating sum on every four-point rectangle is zero. Parametrize the arcs by angles s,t with 0<t−s<2π. Their chord distance is D(s,t)=2sin((t−s)/2), whose mixed derivative is
∂s​∂t​D=21​sin((t−s)/2)>0.
(60)
The zero rectangle identity would force this mixed derivative to vanish, a contradiction. Therefore no such isometry exists.
For a real vector x∈ℓ1n​, list its signed sums over all 2n choices ε∈{−1,1}n, followed by infinitely many zero coordinates:
Tx=(ε⋅x)ε∈{−1,1}n​⊕(0,0,…).

This is linear, has finite support and lies in c0​. Choosing the signs of the components gives maxε​∣ε⋅x∣=∑j​∣xj​∣. Thus ∥Tx∥∞​=∥x∥1​​, the required linear isometry.

On the complex torus C/Λ, the Weierstrass elliptic function ℘ is a degree-two map to the Riemann sphere, and its fibres are the pairs {z,−z}, with coalescence at the four branch points. An even elliptic function is constant on every fibre, so away from those branch points it descends to a meromorphic function Q of ℘.
The descent also holds at a branch point. At a half-period h, evenness and periodicity give f(h+u)=f(h−u), so its local Laurent series uses only even powers of u. Also ℘(h+u)−℘(h) is a local coordinate proportional to u2. At 0, use 1/℘(z)∼z2 instead. Thus Q extends meromorphically across every branch point and infinity. Every meromorphic function on the Riemann sphere is a rational function, proving f=Q∘℘.
For a nonconstant rational function Q=p/q in coprime form, degQ=max(degp,degq): a generic equation p−wq=0 has that many roots on the sphere. Degrees of holomorphic maps multiply under composition. Hence the degree is
degf=2max(degp,degq).​
(62)
Constant functions have degree zero. Degree two therefore occurs exactly when Q is a Möbius transformation:
f(z)=c℘(z)+da℘(z)+b​,ad−bc=0.​
(63)
Conversely every such function is even, elliptic and of degree two.

A parametrization is X(θ,z)=(coshzcosθ,coshzsinθ,z). It gives a homeomorphism S1×R→S, with inverse obtained from the height and angular position. Its first fundamental form is
ds2=cosh2z(dθ2+dz2).
(69)
For a surface of revolution with radius r(z), the Gaussian curvature is −r′′/[r(1+r′2)2]. Thus K=−sech4z<0​. The waist z=0 is a closed geodesic: Γθθz​=−tanhz vanishes there, and θ can be parametrized at constant speed.
For the uniqueness of a closed geodesic on a negatively curved cylinder, use Gauss-Bonnet theorem with piecewise geodesic boundary:
∫D​KdA+∑j​(π−αj​)=2πχ(D).
(70)
A geodesic disk with smooth boundary would require curvature integral 2π. A disk bounded by a geodesic monogon would require π+α>0, and a geodesic bigon would require α+β>0. All are impossible when K<0.
Here is the topological reduction needed to apply this observation without assuming simplicity. Lift a closed geodesic to the universal covering plane of the cylinder. A self-intersection of its lift supplies an innermost monogon by the Jordan curve theorem, so the lift is embedded. A contractible closed geodesic would similarly supply a geodesic disk or monogon, so its winding number is nonzero. Its lift is consequently a proper line, invariant under a nonzero power of the deck translation. Two distinct translates of that line cannot intersect: periodicity would repeat an intersection, and innermost arcs between intersections would bound a bigon. The disjoint translates are ordered transversely, with the deck translation preserving that order. A finite cyclic permutation of this ordered family is impossible, so the lift is invariant under the primitive deck translation too. Thus the original geodesic has a simple image and is at most a repeated traversal of it.
Likewise two distinct simple essential closed geodesics cannot intersect: their periodic lifts would produce a bigon. If disjoint, the Jordan curve theorem on the cylinder says they bound a compact annulus. Its two boundaries have zero geodesic curvature and χ=0, so Gauss-Bonnet gives ∫KdA=0, again impossible. Therefore there is at most one closed geodesic image. Reparametrizations, reversed orientation and multiple traversals are understood to describe the same geometric geodesic.

A measure-preserving transformation is a measurable map T:E→E satisfying μ(T−1A)=μ(A) for every measurable A. An invariant set satisfies T−1A=A (or equality modulo null sets, in the measure-theoretic convention).
Preimages preserve complements and countable unions. Therefore the whole space is invariant, the complement of an invariant set is invariant, and a countable union of invariant sets is invariant. Thus the invariant sets form a σ-algebra. The same proof works modulo null sets because a countable union of null exceptional sets is null.

Now suppose q1​>q2​ and q1​a1​>q2​a2​. Since also p1​<p2​, town 1 has the larger threshold, so t=a1​q1​/p1​. The functions Fs​ are nondecreasing in wealth and in s, and Fs​(x)≥x; these properties follow by induction from the dynamic programming equation.
Prove by induction on the remaining horizon that town 2 is never optimal when continuation is worthwhile. For s=1, the difference between the town values is (q1​−q2​)x+q1​a1​−q2​a2​>0. If a2​≤a1​, monotonicity gives
2q1​​[Fs−1​(x)+Fs−1​(x+2a1​)]>2q2​​[Fs−1​(x)+Fs−1​(x+2a2​)],
(80)
with strictness because the first bracket is positive under the hypotheses.
For a2​>a1​, first suppose x+2a2​≥t. The second town's successful large-reward branch retires, so its value is q2​[Fs−1​(x)+x+2a2​]/2. Town 1 is worth at least q1​[Fs−1​(x)+x+2a1​]/2. Their difference is at least
2q1​−q2​​[Fs−1​(x)+x]+q1​a1​−q2​a2​>0.
(81)
If instead x+2a2​<t, all states after either first-night reward remain below the threshold. By induction a policy starting in town 2 then chooses town 1 on its second night. Its value is
q2​q1​EFs−2​(x+R2​+R1​).
(82)
Interchanging the first two towns gives exactly the same value, because capture probabilities multiply and independent rewards add. After starting in town 1, however, the induction hypothesis says town 2 is strictly inferior on the second night at every possible surviving wealth level. Replacing that second choice by the optimal one strictly improves the value. This proves town 1 dominates throughout every finite horizon.
If a town has pi​=0 and ai​>0, its threshold is interpreted as infinity and retirement is not optimal before the horizon ends. A town with qi​ai​=0 offers no gain; the natural threshold is zero. These conventions handle the degenerate capture probabilities rather than dividing by zero.

When a=0 these zero-eigenvalue events coincide at μ=0, while the off-axis equilibrium also has zero-real-part imaginary eigenvalues for every μ>0.
The centre manifold theorem reduces local dynamics near zero-real-part eigenvalues to an invariant manifold tangent to their eigenspace; transverse directions with nonzero real parts retain their stable or unstable character. For a varying parameter, adjoin μ˙​=0 and use an extended centre manifold for a parameter.
Take a=1. At μ=0 near the origin, y=0 is an exact extended centre manifold. Its reduced equation is
x˙=x2−μ,μ˙​=0.​

This is a saddle-node bifurcation: no nearby axis equilibria for μ<0, one at zero, and two for μ>0. The transverse eigenvalue is positive, so the negative root is a saddle and the positive root an unstable node for small positive μ.
At μ=1, put u=x−1, v=y, ν=μ−1. Then u˙=2u+u2−v−ν, v˙=−uv, ν˙=0. Write the extended centre manifold as u=h(v,ν). Its invariance equation is hv​(−hv)=2h+h2−v−ν. Matching degrees gives

(95)
The exact equilibrium branches are v=0 and v=−ν, crossing at zero and exchanging stability in the centre direction. This is a transcritical bifurcation; the transverse eigenvalue remains positive. For ν<0 the axis branch is an unstable node and the off-axis branch a saddle; for ν>0 their roles reverse locally.
When a=0, the two parameter values merge and the origin at μ=0 has a double zero eigenvalue with nonzero nilpotent linear part. The centre manifold is then two-dimensional, so the preceding one-dimensional classifications cannot simply be reused. Also the off-axis branch has imaginary eigenvalues for every μ>0, with identically zero trace: this is not a generic Hopf bifurcation obtained by varying μ. These degeneracies already follow without computing a new normal form.

ka​=eϕℓa​=∂a​(eϕ).​
(127)
Then ka;b​=eϕ(ℓa;b​+ℓa​ℓb​). Since eϕ=0, the condition on ℓ is exactly ka;b​=0​, so k is a parallel covector field. Closed covectors have this scalar-potential representation locally by the Poincaré lemma; a global potential additionally requires exactness, for example on a simply connected domain.

36E (Fluid Dynamics II)

Words: 89 Articles: 1

Solution

Words: 89
i OurBigBook.com
In a steady axisymmetric flow without swirl, time derivatives and azimuthal derivatives vanish. For a slender high-Reynolds number jet of width δ≪z, radial viscous derivatives dominate axial ones by (z/δ)2. The transverse momentum balance makes pressure nearly constant across the jet, matching the constant ambient pressure, so the leading axial pressure gradient vanishes. Retaining axial convection and radial diffusion in the Navier-Stokes equation gives the boundary-layer equation
ur​∂r​uz​+uz​∂z​uz​=rν​∂r​(r∂r​uz​).​
(128)
The radial velocity is small but its convective term is of the same order as axial convection because radial gradients are larger.

ii

Words: 99 Articles: 1
36E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 99
ii OurBigBook.com
The incompressibility condition turns the left side of the boundary-layer equation into conservative form:
∂z​(uz2​)+r1​∂r​(rur​uz​)=rν​∂r​(r∂r​uz​).
(129)
Multiply by 2πρr and integrate from the axis to infinity. Regularity at the axis and decay in the ambient fluid eliminate the radial boundary terms. Thus the momentum flux is constant,
dzd​(2πρ∫0∞​uz2​rdr)=0.​
(130)
Matching the applied force sets this constant to F. Scaling convection against radial viscosity gives U2/z∼νU/δ2, while the flux gives F∼ρU2δ2. Combining them yields
U(z)∼ρνzF​,δ(z)∼νFρ​​z.​
(131)
The slenderness requirement is δ/z∼νρ/F​≪1, equivalent to a large force-based Reynolds number F/ρ​/ν.

iii

Words: 172 Articles: 1
36E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 172
iii OurBigBook.com
Fix the scaling constants as U=A/z, δ=Bz, with A=F/(ρν) and B=νρ/F​, so AB2=ν. The Stokes streamfunction is then ψ=νzf(η). Write g=f′/η. Differentiation gives
uz​=zA​g,ur​=zAB​(f′−ηf​),∂r​uz​=Bz2A​g′,∂z​uz​=−z2A​(g+ηg′).
(132)
Substitution in the boundary-layer equation, cancelling A2/z3, gives −(f/η)g′−g2=g′′+g′/η. Multiplication by η3 therefore gives the required similarity equation
ff′−η(f′2+ff′′)=f′−ηf′′+η2f′′′.​
(133)
Axis regularity requires zero radial velocity and a finite smooth axial velocity: choose the streamfunction gauge f(0)=0 and require f(η)=cη2+O(η4). Equivalently f′(0)=0, f′/η has a finite limit, and (f′/η)′→0 at the axis. The constant c is not specified in advance. In the quiescent ambient fluid require f′/η→0 and f′−f/η→0 as η→∞, so both velocity components vanish. The localized physical jet has finite axial volume flux, corresponding to finite f(∞).
Finally the prescribed force fixes the amplitude through the finite momentum-flux normalization
2π∫0∞​ηf′(η)2​dη=1.​
(134)
The axis conditions express regularity rather than independently prescribed arbitrary derivatives; the far-field conditions express matching to the resting fluid, and the integral condition supplies the jet strength.

37B (Waves)

Words: 251 Articles: 1
Paper 3 OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 251
37B OurBigBook.com
For the local phase S, define ki​=∂i​S and ω=−∂t​S. The dispersion relation is the Hamilton-Jacobi equation St​+Ω(∇S,x,t)=0. Differentiate it in space and follow a ray with group velocity x˙i​=Ωki​​; symmetry of the phase Hessian cancels the terms involving ∂i​kj​. Thus the ray-tracing equations are
dtdxi​​=Ωki​​,dtdki​​=−Ωxi​​,dtdω​=Ωt​.​
(135)
Here d/dt=∂t​+x˙⋅∇ means differentiation along the moving ray; subscripts on Ω mean partial derivatives holding its other independent arguments fixed.
The depth is stationary and independent of y, so ω=ω∞​ and l are constant. Choose the incident direction with positive l; the other sign reflects the picture. In the far deep water,
κ∞​=ω∞2​/g,l=κ∞​sinθ∞​,k∞​=−κ∞​cosθ∞​.
(136)
Since Ω depends isotropically on the horizontal wavevector, the group-velocity ratio is l/k. Therefore the ray equation is
dxdy​=kl​,k=−κ(x)2−l2​,ω∞2​=gκtanh(καxp).​
(137)
Near shore, κh→0, so the shallow-water dispersion relation gives κ∼ω∞​/(gα​xp/2) and k∼−κ. Integrating the ray slope yields
q=1+2p​,A=−ω∞​(1+p/2)lgα​​=−1+p/2ω∞​α/g​sinθ∞​​.​
(138)
For p<2, the near-shore phase is S∼ly−ω∞​t−ω∞​x1−p/2/[gα​(1−p/2)]. A constant-phase wave crest thus has
y−yc​∼lgα​(1−p/2)ω∞​​x1−p/2.
(139)
Its tangent becomes parallel to the shoreline, while rays approach perpendicular to it. The exponent is between zero and one, giving the curved crests sketched below for p=1.
These are the formal geometrical optics asymptotics. For fixed α and p<2, κx→0 arbitrarily close to the shore, so the slowly varying wave approximation eventually fails there; the sketch describes the ray-theory regime before that final inner region.

a

Words: 154 Articles: 1
38E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 154
a OurBigBook.com
Use u^n(θ)=∑m​umn​e−imθ, initially for finite-support sequences and then by Plancherel theorem for ℓ2. A shift by k multiplies the transform by eikθ. Hence the recurrence gives
A(θ)u^n+1=B(θ)u^n,u^n+1=H(θ)u^n=H(θ)n+1u^0.​
(140)
Here the last equality is understood with time-zero data, and the scheme is assumed well-defined, so the denominator is nonzero or any removable singularity is filled continuously.
If ∣H∣≤1, Plancherel gives ∥un∥2​≤∥u0∥2​ for every n. Conversely, if the continuous amplification factor has ∣H(θ0​)∣>1, it exceeds 1+δ on an interval of positive length. Choose a nonzero initial Fourier transform supported in that interval. Then ∥un∥2​≥(1+δ)n∥u0∥2​, contradicting a uniform stability bound. Therefore uniform power stability holds exactly when
∣H(θ)∣≤1(−π≤θ≤π).​
(141)
Without continuity the exact condition is an essential-supremum bound, since isolated Fourier frequencies have zero measure. The fixed recurrence here uses a bound uniform over all time steps; mesh-dependent finite-time growth bounds are a different stability convention.

b

Words: 52 Articles: 1
38E OurBigBook.com

Solution

Words: 52
b OurBigBook.com
For the Fourier mode ei(iθ+jϕ), the Forward Euler method has amplification factor
H(θ,ϕ)=1−4μ[sin2(θ/2)+csin2(ϕ/2)].
(142)
It is real and ranges from 1−4μ(1+c) to 1. The two-dimensional Fourier stability analysis therefore requires its minimum to be at least −1. Thus the exact stable range is
0<μ≤2(1+c)1​.​
(143)
The endpoint is included; the highest-frequency mode then has amplification −1 and bounded norm.
